screens.title: Integration Testing: Why and How
screens.narratorSegment: Integration testing verifies that multiple contracts work together when they exchange messages and change shared state. Unlike unit tests, which exercise a single contract in isolation, integration tests deploy each dependent contract and exercise the actual inter-contract calls. A clear example is a Vault that relies on an ERC-20 token: the vault's deposit function calls token. transferFrom, so your test must deploy both contracts, transfer tokens to a user, have the user approve the vault, call deposit, and then assert balances and events on both contracts. Integration tests are crucial because they catch mismatches such as an incorrect constructor address, a forgotten approve call, or an assumption about msg. sender that fails when a different account interacts. A common misconception is that unit tests plus code reviews are sufficient; they are not. Integration tests reveal behavioral interactions and event sequences that only appear when contracts run together. To write a reliable integration test, organize a beforeEach that deploys contracts in sequence, use signers to represent different users, and assert across contracts: allowances, token balances, vault deposits, and emitted events. The closing checklist: deploy dependencies, simulate the real two-step token flow, verify states across all contracts, and include negative tests for failure modes.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Integration tests deploy interacting contracts and validate real inter-contract flows such as approve → transferFrom sequences.

content.html:
Core Concept

Integration Testing: Why and How

Integration tests validate interactions between two or more deployed contracts.

What it is
  • Deploy each dependent contract and wire addresses exactly as in production.
  • Simulate full user flows, not just single function behavior.
  • Assert effects across all involved contracts and emitted events.
Common misconception
Unit tests alone often miss cross-contract issues like wrong addresses or missing approvals.
Key Takeaway

Integration tests catch interaction bugs that unit tests cannot, and should assert both state and events across contracts.

Concrete example: Vault + MyToken
Sequence to test:
  1. Deploy MyToken with initial supply and owner.
  2. Deploy Vault and pass MyToken address to its constructor.
  3. Transfer tokens to user, user approves vault, user calls deposit.
  4. Assert token balances, vault deposits mapping, and Deposited event.
Why it matters: this sequence reproduces the actual on-chain lifecycle and validates the system rather than the unit.

screens.title: Deploy Order and beforeEach Fixtures
screens.narratorSegment: Setting up test fixtures with the correct deployment order is a small but critical step in integration testing. The principle is simple: deploy contracts that provide services first, then deploy contracts that depend on them, passing addresses into constructors or setter functions. For example, deploy MyToken first so you can pass its address into Vault's constructor. Implement this in a beforeEach block so each test begins from a fresh, known state. A practical pattern is: retrieve signers, deploy mock or real token, then deploy dependent contracts, then prepare accounts with transfers or approvals. This sequence prevents tests from sharing state and makes each test deterministic. A common mistake is deploying dependent contracts with an incorrect or uninitialized address, which produces a silent failure later when a call is made to a zero address or an unexpected contract. Also check that your deployment transaction is awaited and that deployed() is called where appropriate to ensure the contract is available before use. In tests, after deployment, immediately assert that important references, like vault. token. address, match the deployed token address. This assertion is a small but powerful guard against wiring mistakes. Finally, keep fixtures minimal and only deploy what your test needs; simpler mocks are faster and easier to reason about.

content.html:
Process Flow

Deploy Order and beforeEach Fixtures

A reliable beforeEach deploys contracts in sequence and prepares accounts.

Deployment steps
Step 1 — Signers
Call ethers.getSigners and assign owner, user1, user2.
Step 2 — Deploy Token
Deploy MyToken with initial supply and owner address.
Step 3 — Deploy Vault
Deploy Vault and pass MyToken.address into the constructor.
Step 4 — Prepare Accounts
Transfer tokens to user accounts and assert balances before tests run.
Guards and assertions
  • Await deployment and call deployed() to ensure the contract is ready.
  • Assert dependent contract stores the provider address you passed.
  • Keep fixture scope narrow to speed up the suite and reduce coupling.
Mistake to avoid: deploying contracts in the wrong order or forgetting await leads to flakey tests that fail intermittently.

screens.title: Signer Management and connect()
screens.narratorSegment: Signers let you simulate different accounts interacting with your contracts, which is essential for integration tests. ethers. getSigners returns a list of test accounts you can use as deployer, user, and other roles. The important pattern is to use contract. connect(signer) so that transactions originate from the desired account and msg. sender inside the contract matches that signer. For example, to simulate user1 approving and depositing, call myToken. connect(user1). approve(vault. address, amount) and then vault. connect(user1). deposit(amount). If you forget to connect the correct signer, tests may pass or fail for the wrong reason because transactions will come from the default signer. A concrete mistake is calling myToken. transfer(user1. address, amount) from the owner but then attempting vault. connect(user1). deposit without ensuring user1 has approved; tests can be misleading. Another nuance: approvals and allowances are tied to token holder addresses, so always assert allowance(user1, vault. address) equals the expected value after approve. Signer management also helps you test permissioned functions by attempting restricted calls from unauthorized accounts and asserting they revert. The closing takeaway: always choose signers deliberately, use connect() on every transaction that should come from a particular account, and assert both pre- and post-conditions tied to those accounts to avoid hidden assumptions.

keyIdea.text: Always use contract.connect(signer) for transactions that must come from a specific account, and assert allowances and balances for that signer.

content.html:
Definition

Signer Management and connect()

Use signers to model distinct users and preserve correct msg.sender semantics.

Pattern
// obtain signers
[owner, user1] = await ethers.getSigners();

// user1 approves vault
await myToken.connect(user1).approve(vault.address, amount);

// user1 deposits
await vault.connect(user1).deposit(amount);
This sequence ensures approve and deposit originate from user1 so token allowances and deposits map to the same address.
Checks to add
  • Assert myToken.allowance(user1.address, vault.address) equals approved amount.
  • Assert myToken.balances(user1.address) decreases after deposit.
  • Attempt privileged calls from unauthorized signers and expect revert messages.
Misconception: using the default signer accidentally can hide bugs related to caller identity. Be explicit with connect().

screens.title: Testing approve → transferFrom Flow
screens.narratorSegment: The approve then transferFrom pattern is central to ERC-20 interactions and must be reproduced in your tests. The two-step flow means the token holder first approves a spender for a specific amount, and then the spender calls transferFrom to move tokens. In an integration test this looks like: owner transfers tokens to user, user calls approve to allow the vault to spend, and vault calls transferFrom during deposit. A concrete test will assert the allowance after approve, expect the Deposited event on deposit, and then assert both the token balance and the vault's internal deposit mapping. A common failure mode is skipping approve in tests — transferFrom will revert because allowance is zero, and tests must check that this revert message originates from the token contract. In your test code, present the sequence clearly and assert intermediate state: check allowance immediately after approve, not only after deposit. Also verify that events are emitted with the correct arguments. Finally, when writing the code block in your test, always await transactions and prefer explicit expect(...). to. emit([...]) assertions so the suite both documents and verifies the expected event sequence.

keyIdea.title: Approval Flow
keyIdea.text: Reproduce the approve then transferFrom sequence in tests, assert allowance, emitted events, and balances across token and consumer contracts.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Testing approve → transferFrom Flow

Recreate the approval and transfer lifecycle and assert state at each step.

// Example test snippet (structure shown, escapes applied)
await myToken.connect(owner).transfer(user1.address, depositAmount);

await myToken.connect(user1).approve(vault.address, depositAmount);
expect(await myToken.allowance(user1.address, vault.address)).to.equal(depositAmount);

await expect(vault.connect(user1).deposit(depositAmount))
  .to.emit(vault, "Deposited")
  .withArgs(user1.address, depositAmount);

expect(await myToken.balances(user1.address)).to.equal(initialUserBalance.sub(depositAmount));
expect(await myToken.balances(vault.address)).to.equal(depositAmount);
expect(await vault.deposits(user1.address)).to.equal(depositAmount);
Checklist
  • Transfer tokens to the test user before approve.
  • Assert allowance immediately after approve.
  • Use expect(...).to.emit to verify events on deposit.
Common Mistake

Forgetting approve leads to a revert from transferFrom; ensure tests explicitly simulate both steps.

screens.title: Mocks vs Forking Mainnet
screens.narratorSegment: When testing interactions with common protocols or external contracts you have two main strategies: deploy simplified mock contracts locally or fork an existing network to test against real deployed contracts. Mocks are lightweight, deterministic, and fast. You can implement only the functions your tests need, such as balanceOf, transfer, approve, or a getPrice method for an oracle. Mocks let you control edge conditions and force error responses. Forking mainnet reproduces real contract logic and current state, which is useful when behavior depends on complex production data. But forking is slower, harder to control, and can make tests brittle if external contracts change. The recommended practice for most integration tests in development is to use mocks for unit and integration-level verification, and reserve forking for a small subset of end-to-end tests that must validate integration with third-party protocols. A concrete example: to test a Vault that accepts ERC-20, deploy MyToken mock and assert deposit and withdrawal flows. Reserve a forked test only if you must interact with a real DEX or oracle implementation. Remember: keep mocks minimal and only implement behavior your tests verify; over-complicating mocks can hide A P I mismatches and increase maintenance cost.

keyIdea.text: Mocks are fast and controllable; forking reproduces real state but is slower and brittle. Use mocks for routine integration tests.

content.html:
Comparison

Mocks vs Forking Mainnet

Tradeoffs when testing external dependencies.

Mocks
  • Pros: deterministic, fast, and under your control.
  • Pros: easy to force edge cases and errors.
  • Cons: may diverge from real implementations if over-simplified.
Best for regular integration and unit tests where behavior is simple and known.
Forking
  • Pros: interact with real deployed contracts and current state.
  • Pros: useful for end-to-end verification against established protocols.
  • Cons: slower, requires network config, and can be brittle.
Use sparingly for final integration checks that require real protocol behavior.

screens.title: Cross-Contract Assertions and Events
screens.narratorSegment: A robust integration test checks the state of every contract affected by an operation. When a user deposits tokens into a Vault, you must inspect token balances, the vault's deposits mapping, allowances, and any emitted events. Events are especially valuable because they document the intended external behavior: assert that the Deposited event fired with the correct user and amount. Also verify token-side state: the token's balances mapping should reflect the transfer from user to vault, and allowance should have been reduced if using transferFrom. When designing assertions, think in terms of system invariants: total supply remains constant, vault accounting plus user balances sum accordingly, and events match the numeric changes. A common mistake is only asserting one contract's state; this can hide mismatched logic where one contract updated but the other did not. In your tests, place multiple expect statements: allowances, token balances, vault deposits, and event assertions. Order your assertions logically so failures pinpoint the first mismatch. This practice builds confidence that the system of contracts behaves as a cohesive unit. Cross-Contract Assertions and Events means assert balances, allowances, internal mappings, and events across all contracts touched by a transaction to validate the full interaction.. In practical terms, verifying state across token and consumer contracts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Assert balances, allowances, internal mappings, and events across all contracts touched by a transaction to validate the full interaction.

content.html:
Architecture

Cross-Contract Assertions and Events

Assert each contract's state and emitted events to validate integrated behavior.

Example assertion sequence
  1. Assert myToken.allowance(user1, vault) equals depositAmount after approve.
  2. Expect vault.deposit to emit Deposited(user1, depositAmount).
  3. Assert myToken.balances(user1) decreased by depositAmount.
  4. Assert myToken.balances(vault) increased by depositAmount.
  5. Assert vault.deposits(user1) equals depositAmount.
Check events and state to ensure both sides of the token transfer reflect the operation.
Pro tip
Use expect(...).to.emit with .withArgs to tightly couple event arguments to your assertions and catch mismatches early.
Common Mistake

Relying only on one contract's state can hide a failed transfer or an allowance bug; assert both sides.

screens.title: Mock Contracts: Design and Scope
screens.narratorSegment: Mocks are simplified contract implementations you deploy inside tests to control external behavior. The goal is minimalism: implement only functions your tests call. For an ERC-20 mock you might include balance mappings, transfer, approve, transferFrom, and allowance checks. For an oracle mock, provide a setter to control the price and a getter used by the consumer contract. Minimal mocks let tests be deterministic and easy to maintain. A common trap is over-engineering mocks to fully re-implement a standard; this increases maintenance and may drift from actual protocol behavior. Instead, focus mocks on the exact interface and edge cases your contract expects: return a specific price, or force transferFrom to revert for insufficient allowance. Also add events to mocks if your tests assert them. When designing mocks, document the functions they expose and the intended responses so future test authors understand the controlled scenarios. Finally, include negative mocks that simulate failures to ensure your contract handles reverts gracefully. This balance between simplicity and targeted behavior makes integration tests both reliable and expressive. In practical terms, create minimal mocks for erc-20 and oracles to control behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Mocks are simplified contract implementations you deploy inside tests to control external behavior. The goal is minimalism: implement only functions your tests call. For an ERC-20 mock you might include balance mappings, transfer, approve, transferFrom, and allowance checks. For an oracle mock, provide a setter to control the price and a getter used by the consumer contract. Minimal mocks let tests be deterministic and easy to maintain. A common trap is over-engineering mocks to fully re-implement a standard; this increases maintenance and may drift from actual protocol behavior. Instead, focus mocks on the exact interface and edge cases your contract expects: return a specific price, or force transferFrom to revert for insufficient allowance. Also add events to mocks if your tests assert them. When designing mocks, document the functions they expose and the intended responses so future test authors understand the controlled scenarios. Finally, include negative mocks that simulate failures to ensure your contract handles reverts gracefully. This balance between simplicity and targeted behavior makes integration tests both reliable and expressive. Mock Contracts: Design and Scope means implement only the functions and responses your tests need; keep mocks simple and targeted to test specific behaviors and failure modes.. In practical terms, create minimal mocks for erc-20 and oracles to control behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

Mock Contracts: Design and Scope

Keep mocks focused on the interface and behaviors your tests require.

ERC-20 mock essentials
  • balance mapping and balanceOf method
  • transfer, approve, transferFrom and allowance
  • emit Transfer and Approval events when actions occur
Keep constructor minting and a simple transfer logic for predictable tests.
Oracle mock essentials
  • setter to control price values
  • getter used by consumer contracts
  • ability to simulate stale or erroneous responses
Design negative responses to verify your contract's revert paths and error handling.

screens.title: Testing Failure Modes and Reverts
screens.narratorSegment: Negative tests are as important as positive ones. When a contract calls transferFrom, several failure modes can occur: allowance is zero, balance is insufficient, or the token contract itself reverts. Your integration suite should include tests that intentionally trigger these failures so you can assert revert messages and ensure the consumer contract fails safely. For example, test deposit without prior approve and expect a revert with the token's revert message. Test withdraw when vault. deposits for the user is less than requested and assert the Vault's revert message. Also test edge inputs like zero amounts. When asserting reverts, include the exact revert string from the contract when available; this tells you whether the revert came from the token or from your own contract. Structured negative tests improve maintainability by documenting expected error behavior and avoiding flakiness when future code changes alter error propagation. Finally, if a test expects a revert from a mock, design the mock to revert with a clear message so the test can assert the correct failure reason. Testing Failure Modes and Reverts means write tests that reproduce expected failure modes and assert specific revert messages so failures are intentional and documented.. In practical terms, include negative tests for missing approvals and insufficient balances. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow

Testing Failure Modes and Reverts

Include tests that intentionally trigger and assert revert behavior.

Failure scenarios to test
  • Deposit without approve should revert from the token with allowance error.
  • Withdraw more than deposited should revert with vault's insufficient balance message.
  • Deposit of zero should revert by contract precondition checks.
Assert the origin and text of the revert to distinguish token vs vault failures.
Test pattern
// expect revert due to missing approval
await expect(vault.connect(user1).deposit(amount))
  .to.be.revertedWith("ERC20: transfer amount exceeds allowance");

// expect revert on withdraw too large
await expect(vault.connect(user1).withdraw(amount.add(1)))
  .to.be.revertedWith("Vault: Insufficient balance in vault");

screens.title: Activity: Staking Contract Integration Test
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity asks you to adapt the Vault integration test pattern to a Staking contract that accepts stakes and returns tokens on unstake. Start by deploying MyToken and then Staking, passing the token address into the constructor. Transfer tokens to user1, have user1 approve the Staking contract, then call stake. Assert that myToken. balances(user1) decreases, the staking contract's token balance increases, stakedBalances[user1] increments, and totalStaked increases. Next, test unstake by calling unstake and asserting balances return appropriately and Unstaked is emitted. Add negative tests: stake with amount zero must revert, unstake more than staked must revert, and attempting stake without approval should revert from transferFrom. A useful testing pattern is a full stake-then-unstake cycle where you assert that after unstake all balances and totals match the initial state. These tests mirror the Vault example but exercise a different state variable naming and total accounting, reinforcing the generality of the approach. As you implement each test, await transactions, use connect(signers) to originate actions from user1, and assert both token-side and staking contract state to ensure integrated correctness. Hands-on Activity

Activity: Staking Contract Integration Test

Use the same integration patterns to test a Staking contract.

Starter checklist

  2. Transfer tokens to user1 and assert initial balance.
  3. user1 approves Staking then stakes amount; assert balances and stakedBalances.

screens.title: Test Organization and Speed
screens.narratorSegment: As your integration test suite grows, organization and performance become important. Structure tests so each file focuses on a cohesive feature set, for example Vault tests in one file and Staking tests in another. Use beforeEach fixtures to deploy minimal contracts needed by the tests in that file. Keep mocks small and focused to reduce compile and deploy times. Prefer isolated integration tests that spin up only the contracts required for the scenario rather than deploying an entire protocol graph for every test. Parallelize where your test runner allows it, and group slower forked tests separately so they don't block fast development loops. Add clear test names and comments that explain why a test exists and the invariant it verifies. Use unit tests for internal logic and integration tests for cross-contract behavior; this split keeps both kinds of tests concise. Finally, when you encounter flaky tests, isolate the smallest failing scenario and add explicit assertions about state transitions to make failures diagnostic. Optimizing test structure and speed reduces developer friction and increases confidence that the integrated system is correct. Test Organization and Speed means organize tests by feature, keep fixtures minimal, and separate fast mocks from slow forked end-to-end tests to maintain a fast, reliable suite.. In practical terms, keep your integration suite maintainable and fast. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Best Practices

Test Organization and Speed

Design tests for clarity and fast feedback.

Timeline for a test file
1. Setup signers and minimal mocks
2. Deploy only required contracts
3. Execute positive and negative cases
4. Assert cross-contract invariants
Group slow tests (forks) separately and keep everyday development cycles fast with focused mocks and minimal fixtures.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's review the essential concepts to carry forward. First, integration testing means deploying dependent contracts and asserting their interactions so real on-chain behavior is reproduced. Second, signer management with connect() is vital: always originate transactions from the intended account and check allowances and balances for that signer. Third, design mocks narrowly: implement only the functions and responses your tests require, and create negative responses to validate failure handling. These ideas together let you write tests that both prove correctness and document expected behaviors. Keep tests minimal, assert across all affected contracts, and include negative tests for missing approvals or insufficient balances. When necessary, use a forked network to validate against real protocols, but use it sparingly because it is slower and harder to control. Continue practicing by adapting the Vault pattern to Staking and other consumer contracts to build confidence in multi-contract systems.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on integration testing: exercises that verify how multiple smart contracts behave together. Real DApps are networks of contracts — tokens, vaults, staking, oracles — and your tests must recreate that communication in a controlled environment. You will learn deploy-order patterns, how to use signers to simulate distinct users, and the exact steps to mimic ERC-20 flows like approve then transferFrom. We'll walk through a concrete Vault and Token example, show how to assert cross-contract state and events, and explore mocking strategies for common standards. This matters because an isolated contract test can hide failures that only appear when messages cross contract boundaries. A passing unit test does not guarantee integrated behavior; integration tests catch incorrect addresses, missing approvals, and mistaken caller identities. As you study this chapter, keep in mind a single concrete example: deploy a simplified ERC-20, deploy a Vault with the token address, transfer tokens to a user, have the user approve the Vault, then deposit and withdraw. That small sequence demonstrates the essential lifecycle of inter-contract calls. By the end you should be able to set up beforeEach scaffolding, simulate users with ethers. getSigners, and write assertions that cover both token and vault state. What integrated behavior will you validate first when testing your own DApp?

By the end of these lessons you will be able to write integration tests that deploy multiple smart contracts and verify their interactions. You will set up beforeEach fixtures to deploy tokens and dependent contracts in sequence, and you will simulate different users by using the signers provided by your test framework. You'll also be able to simulate token flows with approve and transferFrom, and write assertions that inspect both token state and dependent contract storage. Finally, you'll learn strategies for testing standard token interfaces by deploying simple mock implementations that you control. These abilities matter: they let you catch real-world failures such as missing approvals, wrong deploy addresses, and incorrect msg. sender assumptions before your contracts are deployed on-chain. You will practice these skills with a Vault and simplified ERC-20 example, and then extend the approach to staking patterns and oracle-driven systems. A verified competency milestone on each card links the objective to a measurable test you should be able to write.

This second set of objectives ties each skill to a practical test you will write. First, you will produce a beforeEach that sequentially deploys a mock ERC-20 and then a dependent contract, demonstrating correct address wiring. Second, you will write tests that use at least two signers to show transactions coming from different accounts, ensuring msg. sender behavior is correct. Third, you will implement tests that intentionally fail when approve is missing, proving your suite detects missing allowances. Fourth, you will create simple mock contracts for tokens or oracles so you can force specific responses and verify error handling. Each milestone is measurable by assertions: event emissions, balance changes, and reverted messages. These outcomes are important because they map directly to proof that your multi-contract system functions as intended. When you can produce these tests consistently, you reduce deployment risk and make debugging much faster in complex integrations.

Integration testing verifies that multiple contracts work together when they exchange messages and change shared state. Unlike unit tests, which exercise a single contract in isolation, integration tests deploy each dependent contract and exercise the actual inter-contract calls. A clear example is a Vault that relies on an ERC-20 token: the vault's deposit function calls token. transferFrom, so your test must deploy both contracts, transfer tokens to a user, have the user approve the vault, call deposit, and then assert balances and events on both contracts. Integration tests are crucial because they catch mismatches such as an incorrect constructor address, a forgotten approve call, or an assumption about msg. sender that fails when a different account interacts. A common misconception is that unit tests plus code reviews are sufficient; they are not. Integration tests reveal behavioral interactions and event sequences that only appear when contracts run together. To write a reliable integration test, organize a beforeEach that deploys contracts in sequence, use signers to represent different users, and assert across contracts: allowances, token balances, vault deposits, and emitted events. The closing checklist: deploy dependencies, simulate the real two-step token flow, verify states across all contracts, and include negative tests for failure modes.

Setting up test fixtures with the correct deployment order is a small but critical step in integration testing. The principle is simple: deploy contracts that provide services first, then deploy contracts that depend on them, passing addresses into constructors or setter functions. For example, deploy MyToken first so you can pass its address into Vault's constructor. Implement this in a beforeEach block so each test begins from a fresh, known state. A practical pattern is: retrieve signers, deploy mock or real token, then deploy dependent contracts, then prepare accounts with transfers or approvals. This sequence prevents tests from sharing state and makes each test deterministic. A common mistake is deploying dependent contracts with an incorrect or uninitialized address, which produces a silent failure later when a call is made to a zero address or an unexpected contract. Also check that your deployment transaction is awaited and that deployed() is called where appropriate to ensure the contract is available before use. In tests, after deployment, immediately assert that important references, like vault. token. address, match the deployed token address. This assertion is a small but powerful guard against wiring mistakes. Finally, keep fixtures minimal and only deploy what your test needs; simpler mocks are faster and easier to reason about.

Signers let you simulate different accounts interacting with your contracts, which is essential for integration tests. ethers. getSigners returns a list of test accounts you can use as deployer, user, and other roles. The important pattern is to use contract. connect(signer) so that transactions originate from the desired account and msg. sender inside the contract matches that signer. For example, to simulate user1 approving and depositing, call myToken. connect(user1). approve(vault. address, amount) and then vault. connect(user1). deposit(amount). If you forget to connect the correct signer, tests may pass or fail for the wrong reason because transactions will come from the default signer. A concrete mistake is calling myToken. transfer(user1. address, amount) from the owner but then attempting vault. connect(user1). deposit without ensuring user1 has approved; tests can be misleading. Another nuance: approvals and allowances are tied to token holder addresses, so always assert allowance(user1, vault. address) equals the expected value after approve. Signer management also helps you test permissioned functions by attempting restricted calls from unauthorized accounts and asserting they revert. The closing takeaway: always choose signers deliberately, use connect() on every transaction that should come from a particular account, and assert both pre- and post-conditions tied to those accounts to avoid hidden assumptions.

The approve then transferFrom pattern is central to ERC-20 interactions and must be reproduced in your tests. The two-step flow means the token holder first approves a spender for a specific amount, and then the spender calls transferFrom to move tokens. In an integration test this looks like: owner transfers tokens to user, user calls approve to allow the vault to spend, and vault calls transferFrom during deposit. A concrete test will assert the allowance after approve, expect the Deposited event on deposit, and then assert both the token balance and the vault's internal deposit mapping. A common failure mode is skipping approve in tests — transferFrom will revert because allowance is zero, and tests must check that this revert message originates from the token contract. In your test code, present the sequence clearly and assert intermediate state: check allowance immediately after approve, not only after deposit. Also verify that events are emitted with the correct arguments. Finally, when writing the code block in your test, always await transactions and prefer explicit expect(...). to. emit([...]) assertions so the suite both documents and verifies the expected event sequence.

When testing interactions with common protocols or external contracts you have two main strategies: deploy simplified mock contracts locally or fork an existing network to test against real deployed contracts. Mocks are lightweight, deterministic, and fast. You can implement only the functions your tests need, such as balanceOf, transfer, approve, or a getPrice method for an oracle. Mocks let you control edge conditions and force error responses. Forking mainnet reproduces real contract logic and current state, which is useful when behavior depends on complex production data. But forking is slower, harder to control, and can make tests brittle if external contracts change. The recommended practice for most integration tests in development is to use mocks for unit and integration-level verification, and reserve forking for a small subset of end-to-end tests that must validate integration with third-party protocols. A concrete example: to test a Vault that accepts ERC-20, deploy MyToken mock and assert deposit and withdrawal flows. Reserve a forked test only if you must interact with a real DEX or oracle implementation. Remember: keep mocks minimal and only implement behavior your tests verify; over-complicating mocks can hide A P I mismatches and increase maintenance cost.

A robust integration test checks the state of every contract affected by an operation. When a user deposits tokens into a Vault, you must inspect token balances, the vault's deposits mapping, allowances, and any emitted events. Events are especially valuable because they document the intended external behavior: assert that the Deposited event fired with the correct user and amount. Also verify token-side state: the token's balances mapping should reflect the transfer from user to vault, and allowance should have been reduced if using transferFrom. When designing assertions, think in terms of system invariants: total supply remains constant, vault accounting plus user balances sum accordingly, and events match the numeric changes. A common mistake is only asserting one contract's state; this can hide mismatched logic where one contract updated but the other did not. In your tests, place multiple expect statements: allowances, token balances, vault deposits, and event assertions. Order your assertions logically so failures pinpoint the first mismatch. This practice builds confidence that the system of contracts behaves as a cohesive unit.
